label: Living in Berlin
lede: I write these for people who already live here, not for people passing through. Every guide starts from a Berlin date, a Berlin price or a Berlin rule that just moved, and ends with the one thing I would actually do about it.
shelfLegend: By the part of life it hits
shelfLegendSub: Four shelves, because that is how the questions actually arrive

lead.title: Rundfunkbeitrag in Berlin: One Flat, One Fee, and Four Ways to Pay Twice
lead.excerpt: One flat, one contribution, 18.36 euro a month, whoever lives there and whatever they own. In a city where 977,000 households hold a single person that lands harder than anywhere else. Here is who owes it, the four places Berliners quietly pay twice, and the exemptions that are never granted automatically.
lead.alt: The main entrance of the Haus des Rundfunks on Masurenallee in Berlin-Charlottenburg, gold lettering above a brick and glass doorway with people walking in
lead.line: a month per flat, whoever lives there, and four places Berliners quietly pay it twice.

glossary.title: Berlin Rent Increase: Which of the Four Limits Actually Stops the Letter
glossary.alt: A Gruenderzeit apartment building on Hermannstrasse in Berlin-Neukoelln, with red brick and stucco ornament above the ground floor windows and blue sky reflected in the panes
glossary.gloss: The rent table your increase letter is built on. The median net cold rent sits at 7.71 euro per square metre, and four separate limits decide whether the letter holds up.

glossary.title: Berlin Nebenkostenabrechnung: How to Check the Bill Line by Line Before the Deadline
glossary.alt: The yellow corner Altbau at Weserstrasse 58 and Wildenbruchstrasse 87 in Berlin-Neukölln with parked cars along both streets
glossary.gloss: The yearly statement that says what your flat really cost. Two twelve-month deadlines decide whether it still counts, and the city publishes what every line normally costs per square metre.

glossary.title: Berlin Heating Season: What Your Landlord Owes You When the Flat Goes Cold
glossary.alt: A lit Altbau entrance on Handjerystrasse in Berlin-Friedenau at night, with snow on the hedges and the front steps
glossary.gloss: The heating season, and the reason your landlord owes you something at a particular hour. Four of the last eleven autumns crossed the cold snap threshold before it even began.

glossary.title: Health Insurance in Berlin: Which Krankenkasse You Can Actually Join and What the Gap Costs
glossary.alt: The AOK administration tower on Wilhelmstrasse in Berlin-Kreuzberg, a 1960s high-rise by Hans Scharoun and Bodo Fleischer, with the green AOK logo near the roof and a lower wing in front of it
glossary.gloss: The part of statutory health insurance that is not the same everywhere. It runs from 2.18 to 4.39 per cent, and only seven of the 46 funds open to a Berlin address match the ministry's own reference figure.

glossary.title: German Courses in Berlin: What a Lesson Costs and Why the Rules Change at B1
glossary.alt: Volkshochschule Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg in the Wassertorstrasse, a four-storey brick school building on a Kreuzberg street
glossary.gloss: The adult education centre. Up to B1 the price of a German lesson is capped by a federal number and nobody gets a discount. Above B1 the cap disappears and the discounts come back.

glossary.title: Berlin Bulky Waste: What Sperrmüll Costs and Where It Actually Goes
glossary.alt: Orange BSR containers and glass banks lined up inside the recycling yard on Ilsenburger Strasse in Berlin-Charlottenburg
glossary.gloss: Bulky waste. Three cubic metres is the number that decides everything, partial unloading is not allowed, and the pavement version now starts at 300 euro.

glossary.title: Berlin Bridge Days 2027: The Brückentage Worth Booking
glossary.alt: An S-Bahn train pulling out of Berlin Hauptbahnhof past an almost empty platform, with the station name sign lit above the tracks
glossary.gloss: The bridge days. Only six of Berlin's ten public holidays fall on a working day next year, and every one of them lands before 18 May, so the leave you book now decides your spring.

glossary.title: Kleingarten in Berlin: Where the 70,000 Plots Are and How the Wait Really Works
glossary.alt: Sunrise in morning fog over the main path of the Feierabend allotment colony in Berlin-Mariendorf, with hedges and garden gates on both sides
glossary.gloss: The allotment. 70,390 plots in 1,038 colonies, waiting lists run by the colonies themselves, and a takeover price nobody quotes up front.
